the majority of microbial activity and biomass in marine sediments occurs below 20 mbsf.
the subsurface of marine sediments is a habitat of active bacteria and the majority of their biomass.
the majority of bacteria and bacterial activity in deep, low organic matter sediments of the Woodlark basin occur in subsurface layers, and that acetate is an important substrate in this environment.

the distribution of microbial life in marine sediments and the factors that influence this distribution.
the geomicrobiology of deep marine sediments.
the role of microorganisms and their interactions with other biotic and abiotic components of their environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bacterial cells, activity and the potential for activity were widespread throughout the sediments at Sites 1107, 1109, 1115 and 1118.
bacterial populations and activity are present to great depths in deep marine sediments.
the deep subsurface sediments of the Woodlark basin, Pacific Ocean, have a significant bacterial biomass and activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
deep bacterial populations are present and active in the subsurface of deep ocean sediments.
deep subsurface bacterial populations are present and active in the majority of ocean sediments, with acetate being the major substrate for methanogenic activity.
deep, low organic matter sediments in the Pacific Ocean contain active bacterial populations and that acetate is an important substrate for subsurface methanogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are deep subsurface bacteria in the ocean.
the subsurface biosphere is more extensive than previously thought.
there is a significant amount of life in the deep subsurface, even in areas of the world that are relatively devoid of organic matter.
